newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia earns belief in its economy - Merrill.
newsitem.headline: Croatia earns belief in its economy - Merrill.

text.p: Croatia had earned recognition for its efforts to develop its post-war economy, and could soon see a jump in investment, a senior official with U.S. investment house Merrill Lynch said on Tuesday.
"Croatia has considerable resources and people believe in it," Pascal Najadi, vice president in charge of Croatia at Merrill Lynch International, told Reuters in an interview.
"Its economic stability programme is sound. It is perceived internationally to be on track."

Following a recent roadshow to promote a $300 million maiden Eurobond issue through Asia, the United States and Europe, Najadi said he believed the country would soon see a large increase in all forms of investment.
After assisting the ex-communist country to get investment grade credit ratings, and arrange bond issues, Merrill would seek to draw foreign investment to flagship sectors.
Other than just arranging new bond issues, it was considering comprehensive support, from loans to finding direct investors for various sectors, Najadi said.
Because of war following Croatia's independence from former Yugoslavia, direct investments in industry have been slow in coming, totalling just under $250 million in the first nine months last year.
So far they have focused on areas such as cement works, with good immediate prospects thanks to large-scale rebuilding projects, and production of beer, where the market was also poised to rise.
"It is time to deepen the market through reaching all sectors of the economy," Najadi said.
"We are now looking at the industry, where shipbuilding has a very bright future...and there may also be some privatisation issues in the food-processing sector, telecoms..."

Shipbuilding was the leading export trade in Croatia when it was part of Yugoslavia and, along with tourism, its biggest foreign currency earner. But 4-1/2 years of ethnic bloodshed brought both to a virtual halt.
With the additional burden of significant old debts that have since been taken over by government, shipyards struggled to survive and are only now beginning to recover in earnest.
With financial backing for new orders and good quality of ships that had made them renowned worldwide, the industry could get back on its feet pretty soon, Najadi said.
This year might see the first steps in privatising state-owned utilities after the government announced a flotation of the Adriatic oil pipeline.
Profitable telecommunications firm HPT also seems among the more attractive bait for foreign buyers, who will probably be allowed to acquire up to one third in these companies.
Whether through joint ventures or partial sell-off, Croatia will probably need substantial funding to invest in all other utilities in the years ahead.
Najadi said power production facilities, oil and gas exploration and terminals offer but a few of a number of versatile opportunities to foreign investors.
"Croatia is not a reconstruction but an infrastructure story. Now is the right time to develop it," he added.
